message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree—lions are carnivores (Felidae, order Carnivora) while zebras are odd‑toed ungulates (Equidae, order Perissodactyla).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two orders, which lies deep within the clade **Laurasiatheria** (the crown group that also contains Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc.).  

That ancestor was a small, generalized mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous/early Paleocene. It was not a lion or a zebra, but a primitive mammal that gave rise to the lineages that eventually produced the diverse carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates we see today.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the entire clade that includes both Feliformia and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria? Actually Felidae is part of Laurasiatheria (Crown group). Equidae also part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of the two would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc. That ancestor would be a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. But maybe the question expects "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria." But the question might be simpler: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" The answer: "They share a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage, specifically the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria clade, which existed around 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals." But we can mention that the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria, which lived about 70-80 million years ago. Alternatively, we could say "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria."
